newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Global telephone rate system obsolete, ITU says.
newsitem.headline: Global telephone rate system obsolete, ITU says.

text.p: The global accounting rate system that sets telephone call charges between nations is obsolete and should be scrapped eventually, the head of the world's telephone regulator said on Wednesday.

Pekka Tarjanne, secretary general of the International Telecommunication Union (ITU), told Reuters the accounting rates should be replaced by a system based on market forces which more closely reflected the real cost of making a call.
In his strongest criticism of the present system so far, Tarjanne said international rates were too high and any new system would inevitably lead to much lower phone charges.
"Even the lowest rates in the world today are too high. They're well above real costs," he said in an interview at the Asia Telecom 97 trade fair.
"I'm sure they will fall further during the next five years. "Everybody's goal is lower rates," he said.
But, he said; "The accounting rate system is now obsolete. The hope is to create an equitable system, cost based and in agreement with market forces."
Tarjanne said the new system had to be multilateral and would have to be negotiated.
"It is a question of years rather than months," said Tarjanne, whose nine-year term as ITU chief will be over at the end of next year.

An ITU official, who asked not to be identified, said Tarjanne's main aim was to establish a system that would eliminate grossly inflated profit margins from international telephony which were often in excess of 500 percent of costs.

When someone makes an international phone call, they pay their local telephone operator and the accounting rate system was designed to compensate the telephone company in the recipient country for the completion of the call.

It worked well when calls were only made between giant national or international monopolies. But deregulation has opened up markets all over the world and new technology allows users to chose which end of the call to bill.
"Callback" firms allow callers to reverse charges to the cheaper end of any international call and the Internet network of computers allows users to make those calls at local rates.
"A lot of international telecom traffic now flows outside of the formal accounting rate system," Tarjanne said.

"Today, traffic from country A to country B can be five or more times the traffic from country B to country A," he said. "This situation could not have been foreseen when the old accounting rate system was agreed."
The new technology and callbacks have created a huge imbalance in the number of outgoing and incoming calls in the United States.
An immediate scrapping of the system would lead to chaos and would be unfair to many of the world's poorer countries, he said.
In 1995, outgoing calls outnumbered incoming calls by 8.64 billion minutes, according to official figures. U.S. carriers paid out $5.1 billion to foreign telecom companies.

So in December the U.S. regulator, the Federal Communications Commission (FCC), proposed a unilateral cut of around 50 percent in its accounting rate, raising protests from many telecommunications companies around the world.
Tarjanne said unilateral action was not the best way forward and the alternative was not a "sender keeps all" system.
"That would be very detrimental to receivers," he said.
-- Singapore newsroom (65-870-3080)
